commands.name: lsblk
commands.summary: List block devices in a tree view showing partitions and mount points.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
commands.explanation: lsblk displays block devices (disks, partitions, LVM, NVMe) in a tree structure with sizes, types, and mount points. Far clearer than parsing fdisk or df output for understanding disk layout. The -f flag adds filesystem and UUID info.

flags.desc: Show filesystem type, UUID, and label
Don't show device dependencies (list disks only)

examples.desc: Tree view of all block devices
Include filesystem type, UUID, and mount points
List disks with rotation (HDD vs SSD)

commands.pro_tip: Check `ROTA` column in `lsblk -d -o NAME,SIZE,ROTA` — ROTA=1 means HDD (spinning), ROTA=0 means SSD/NVMe. Critical for setting correct I/O scheduler and benchmark expectations.

commands.name: mount
commands.summary: Mount filesystems to make them accessible.
commands.risk_reason: Incorrect mounts can overwrite mountpoints or expose data.
cautions: Mounting over a non-empty directory hides its contents until it is unmounted.
Wrong options (remount,ro, -o bind) can break running services; `umount -l` leaves processes with stale handles.
Test /etc/fstab changes before rebooting — a bad line can drop the machine into emergency mode (add nofail where appropriate).
commands.explanation: mount attaches filesystems (block devices, network shares, virtual filesystems) to the directory tree. Without arguments, shows all currently mounted filesystems. Persistent mounts are configured in /etc/fstab.

flags.desc: Bind-mount a directory to another location

examples.desc: Show all mounts in table format

safer.why: Fake run: shows what `mount -a` would do without mounting anything.

commands.pro_tip: Use `mount -o remount,ro /` for emergency read-only remount during disk issue investigation — prevents further writes while you diagnose. Reverse with `remount,rw`.

commands.name: lvm
commands.summary: Logical Volume Manager: create, resize, and manage logical volumes.
commands.risk_reason: LVM operations on wrong volumes cause data loss.
cautions: Removing or reducing logical volumes destroys data — shrink the filesystem first and keep a snapshot or backup.
Save metadata with vgcfgbackup before big changes.
Check device names with lsblk — pvcreate/pvremove on the wrong disk wipes it.
commands.explanation: LVM abstracts physical storage into volume groups (VGs) and logical volumes (LVs) that can be resized live. The core workflow: create physical volumes (PVs) → group into VGs → carve out LVs. LVs can be snapshotted, resized online, and moved between physical disks.

examples.desc: Show physical volumes, volume groups, and logical volumes
Create a 10GB logical volume named 'data' in vg0
Extend LV by 5GB and grow filesystem
Create a snapshot of a logical volume
Add a new disk to an existing volume group

commands.pro_tip: Create LVM snapshots before risky operations: `lvcreate -s -L 2G -n pre_upgrade /dev/vg0/root` — if something goes wrong, revert instantly with `lvconvert --merge /dev/vg0/pre_upgrade`.

commands.name: mdadm
commands.risk_reason: Incorrect mdadm operations can destroy RAID arrays and data.
cautions: Failing or removing a member of a degraded array can lose the array — check /proc/mdstat first.
--zero-superblock and --create can destroy existing RAID metadata.
Replace one disk at a time and wait for the resync to finish.
commands.explanation: mdadm creates and manages Linux software RAID (md) arrays — RAID 0, 1, 5, 6, and 10. Used on servers without hardware RAID controllers. Key operations: creating arrays, checking sync status, replacing failed drives, and monitoring array health.

examples.desc: Show RAID array status and member disks
Quick RAID sync status and health overview
Remove a failed disk from array

safer.why: Check the array state before any change.

commands.pro_tip: Monitor RAID health with `mdadm --monitor --mail=admin@example.com --daemonise /dev/md0` — sends email on array events. Also check `/proc/mdstat` daily in your monitoring stack.

commands.name: swap
commands.summary: Manage swap space on Linux systems.
commands.risk_reason: Disabling swap on memory-constrained systems triggers OOM.
cautions: Disabling swap on a memory-constrained host can trigger the OOM killer.
swapoff has to move pages back into RAM and can take a long time on a busy system.
Persist swap in /etc/fstab or it disappears at reboot.
commands.explanation: Linux swap (managed via swapon/swapoff and /etc/fstab) extends virtual memory using disk space. On cloud instances, swap files are often preferred over swap partitions. Kubernetes nodes should have swap disabled (swapoff -a) for proper resource accounting.

examples.desc: Show active swap devices and their usage
Create and enable a 4GB swap file
Disable all swap permanently (required for Kubernetes nodes)
Reduce swap aggressiveness (0-100, lower = prefer RAM)

commands.pro_tip: Set `vm.swappiness=10` on database servers — reduces aggressive swap usage that causes latency spikes. On Kubernetes nodes, set `swappiness=0` or disable swap entirely.

commands.name: fdisk
commands.risk_reason: Writing a partition table can destroy all data on the disk.
cautions: Identify the right disk with lsblk and serial numbers before editing.
Nothing is written until w; q quits without saving.
Deleting a partition makes its data unrecoverable without special tools.
Back up the partition table first: sfdisk -d /dev/sdX > sdX.pt
commands.explanation: Interactive tool to create/delete partitions on MBR/GPT disks. Changes are written only when you press w.

commands.name: parted
commands.risk_reason: Applies changes immediately; wrong device or range destroys data.
cautions: mklabel wipes the partition table — all data becomes inaccessible.
-s skips confirmations.
Verify the device with lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,MODEL,SERIAL.
commands.explanation: Create, resize and delete partitions, supports GPT and large disks. Many commands act at once in script mode.

flags.desc: Create a new partition table (destroys existing)

examples.cmd: parted -s /dev/sdb mklabel gpt mkpart primary ext4 0% 100%

commands.name: mkfs
commands.risk_reason: Formats a device — all existing data is lost.
cautions: Irreversible: the old filesystem’s data is overwritten/lost.
Triple-check the device with lsblk -f; a mounted device should never be formatted.
Never run on a device you have not verified is empty (blkid shows existing filesystems).
commands.explanation: Builds a filesystem (mkfs.ext4, mkfs.xfs, mkfs.btrfs …) on a partition or LV.

safer.why: Check whether it already holds a filesystem

commands.name: blkid
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
commands.explanation: Prints UUIDs, labels and filesystem types — use UUIDs in fstab.

commands.name: findmnt
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
commands.explanation: Tree/list view of mounts; --verify checks fstab.

commands.name: umount
commands.risk_reason: Unmounting a busy filesystem can break services; -l/-f leave stale handles or lose data.
cautions: Check usage with fuser -vm / lsof +D first.
Lazy unmount hides problems rather than solving them.
commands.explanation: Detaches a filesystem. Fails if files are open (use lsof/fuser to find them).

flags.desc: Lazy unmount: detach now, clean up later

commands.name: e2fsck
commands.risk_reason: Running fsck on a mounted filesystem can corrupt it; repairs can delete data.
cautions: Never run on a mounted filesystem (except -n).
Take an image backup (dd/ddrescue) of failing disks before repairing.
Repairs can move data to lost+found.
commands.explanation: Checks and repairs ext filesystems. Always run on unmounted devices.

flags.caution: May delete or truncate damaged files.

commands.name: fsck
commands.risk_reason: Repairs can delete or relocate data; running on a mounted filesystem corrupts it.
cautions: Unmount first (or boot rescue mode).
-y can discard data automatically.
Image a failing disk before running repairs.
commands.explanation: Front-end for filesystem checkers (fsck.ext4, fsck.xfs …).

commands.name: xfs_repair
commands.risk_reason: Can discard metadata and data; -L destroys the log.
cautions: Mount/unmount once to replay the log before using -L.
Back up (xfs_metadump or image) before repairs.
commands.explanation: Repairs XFS filesystems, which must be unmounted. -n only checks.

commands.name: resize2fs
commands.risk_reason: Shrinking a filesystem without a backup can corrupt data.
cautions: Shrink the filesystem BEFORE shrinking the LV/partition, never after.
Back up first and run e2fsck -f.
commands.explanation: Grows or shrinks ext2/3/4. Growing can be done online; shrinking needs unmount and fsck.

safer.why: Extend LV + filesystem in one step

commands.name: xfs_growfs
commands.risk_reason: Growing is generally safe, but XFS cannot be shrunk.
cautions: XFS cannot be shrunk — plan sizes carefully.
Ensure the underlying LV/partition has really been extended.
commands.explanation: Expands XFS to fill the underlying device.

commands.name: smartctl
commands.risk_reason: Read-only unless self-tests are started.
cautions: Long self-tests add I/O load — schedule off-peak.
commands.explanation: Reads SMART data: health, error counts, wear and temperature.

commands.name: hdparm
commands.risk_reason: Setting parameters or secure erase can brick or wipe a disk.
cautions: Never use write/security options on the wrong disk.
ATA secure erase destroys all data.
commands.explanation: Queries disk info and benchmarks; can change power, cache and security features.

commands.name: dd
commands.risk_reason: Writing to the wrong target overwrites disks irrecoverably; there is no confirmation.
cautions: Swapping if= and of= overwrites your source.
Triple-check of=/dev/sdX with lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,MODEL,MOUNTPOINT.
Never write to a mounted disk or a device with unknown contents.
Nothing is asked: the first block is overwritten immediately.
commands.explanation: Copies blocks from input to output — used for disk images, boot media and benchmarking.

flags.caution: A wrong of= overwrites data with no prompt.

examples.cmd: dd if=ubuntu.iso of=/dev/sdX bs=4M status=progress conv=fsync
examples.desc: Write an ISO to a USB stick

commands.name: wipefs
commands.risk_reason: Removes filesystem/RAID/LVM signatures; data becomes unreachable.
cautions: Verify the device with lsblk; use -n first.
Back up signatures: wipefs -b …
commands.explanation: Lists or erases signatures from block devices.

commands.name: cryptsetup
commands.risk_reason: Wrong commands destroy the key slots or format the volume; losing the passphrase loses the data.
cautions: Back up the LUKS header immediately after luksFormat — header corruption means total data loss.
Keep at least two key slots/passphrases and store the recovery key safely.
luksFormat erases the target device’s data.
commands.explanation: Sets up, opens and manages LUKS encrypted volumes.

commands.name: pvcreate
commands.summary: Initialize a physical volume for LVM
commands.risk_reason: Writes LVM metadata to the device, destroying existing data.
cautions: Destroys the existing signature on the device.
Check lsblk -f first; never run on a disk with data you need.
commands.explanation: Marks a block device as an LVM PV. See the flags and examples below, and run `man pvcreate` for the full reference.

commands.name: vgcreate
commands.risk_reason: Allocates devices to a volume group.
cautions: Mixing slow/fast or non-redundant disks affects the entire VG.
commands.explanation: Creates a VG from PVs. See the flags and examples below, and run `man vgcreate` for the full reference.

commands.name: lvcreate
commands.risk_reason: Consumes VG space; mis-sizing causes problems later.
cautions: Snapshots that fill up become invalid and degrade performance — monitor with lvs.
commands.explanation: Creates LVs, snapshots and thin volumes.

commands.name: lvextend
commands.risk_reason: Growing is generally safe; wrong args can exhaust the VG.
cautions: Check free VG space (vgs) first.
commands.explanation: Adds space to an LV; use -r to grow the filesystem as well.

commands.name: lvreduce
commands.risk_reason: Shrinking below the filesystem size destroys data.
cautions: Back up first; XFS cannot be shrunk.
Shrink the filesystem before the LV, never after.
commands.explanation: Reduces the size of an LV. The filesystem must be shrunk first.

safer.why: -r shrinks filesystem and LV in the right order

commands.name: lvremove
commands.risk_reason: Deletes the LV and its data.
cautions: Data is gone once removed — snapshot or back up first.
-f skips the confirmation.
commands.explanation: Removes an LV (or snapshot). See the flags and examples below, and run `man lvremove` for the full reference.

commands.name: nfs
commands.risk_reason: Network mounts can hang processes when the server is unavailable; exports can expose data.
cautions: Use hard,intr/soft carefully: soft can silently lose writes, hard can hang processes.
Restrict exports by host and use root_squash; avoid no_root_squash.
Mount with nosuid,nodev,noexec where possible.
commands.explanation: Mount NFS shares with mount -t nfs and export with /etc/exports and exportfs.

commands.name: ddrescue
commands.risk_reason: Writes an image; wrong output target overwrites data.
cautions: Always write to a different disk with enough space.
Never run on a mounted failing disk if you can avoid it.
commands.explanation: GNU ddrescue copies data from failing drives while keeping a map of bad areas.

commands.name: blockdev
commands.risk_reason: Setting flags can make disks read-only/read-write unexpectedly.
cautions: --setrw on a protected device can lead to corruption.
commands.explanation: Query or set block-device parameters. See the flags and examples below, and run `man blockdev` for the full reference.

commands.name: partprobe
commands.risk_reason: Triggers kernel rescans.
cautions: Can disrupt devices in use; prefer partx -u.
commands.explanation: Informs the kernel of partition changes.

commands.name: sfdisk
commands.risk_reason: Writes partition tables non-interactively.
cautions: Restoring writes immediately and destroys the current table.
commands.explanation: Dump/restore partition tables. See the flags and examples below, and run `man sfdisk` for the full reference.

commands.name: tune2fs
commands.risk_reason: Changing features/reserved blocks affects filesystem behaviour.
cautions: Enabling/disabling features on mounted filesystems can corrupt data.
commands.explanation: Tune ext2/3/4 parameters; -l lists them.

commands.name: xfs_info
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
commands.explanation: Prints XFS filesystem parameters. See the flags and examples below, and run `man xfs_info` for the full reference.

commands.name: btrfs
commands.risk_reason: Balance, scrub and delete operations are heavy; subvolume deletion removes data.
cautions: `balance` is I/O heavy; `subvolume delete` removes data.
RAID5/6 is still considered unreliable.
commands.explanation: Manage btrfs subvolumes, snapshots and balancing.

commands.name: zfs
commands.risk_reason: destroy/rollback delete data.
cautions: `zfs destroy` and `zfs rollback` are irreversible; -r destroys children.
Snapshot before risky operations.
commands.explanation: Manage datasets, snapshots, clones. See the flags and examples below, and run `man zfs` for the full reference.

commands.name: zpool
commands.risk_reason: Wrong vdev operations destroy pools.
cautions: `zpool destroy`, `labelclear` and vdev removal can lose the pool.
Mirrors/raidz cannot always be shrunk.
commands.explanation: Manage pools and vdevs. See the flags and examples below, and run `man zpool` for the full reference.

commands.name: rclone
commands.risk_reason: sync deletes destination files.
cautions: `sync` makes the destination identical — a wrong direction erases the source of truth.
Always run with --dry-run first.
commands.explanation: rsync for cloud storage. See the flags and examples below, and run `man rclone` for the full reference.

commands.name: restic
commands.risk_reason: forget --prune deletes snapshots.
cautions: Keep the repository password safe — without it backups are unreadable.
`forget --prune` deletes data; use --dry-run first.
commands.explanation: Deduplicated encrypted backup tool. See the flags and examples below, and run `man restic` for the full reference.

commands.name: borg
commands.risk_reason: prune/delete remove archives.
cautions: Use --dry-run for prune; protect the passphrase and key export.
commands.explanation: Borg backup. See the flags and examples below, and run `man borg` for the full reference.
